question:
Choose the sentence in which the modifier is correctly placed:
A) Walking along the beach, a crab pinched my toe.
B) A crab pinched my toe, walking along the beach.
C) Walking along the beach, I was pinched on the toe by a crab.
D) My toe was pinched by a crab while walking along the beach, I.

options.A: Walking along the beach, a crab pinched my toe.
options.B: A crab pinched my toe, walking along the beach.
options.C: Walking along the beach, I was pinched on the toe by a crab.
options.D: My toe was pinched by a crab while walking along the beach, I.

explanation: The participial phrase 'Walking along the beach' must modify the subject of the main clause. Only in C is the subject 'I' the one who is walking. In A and B, the phrase illogically implies the crab was walking along the beach.

question:
Choose the sentence in which 'only' is placed correctly to convey the intended meaning that Raza eats at that restaurant on no day other than Friday:
A) Raza only eats at that restaurant on Fridays.
B) Only Raza eats at that restaurant on Fridays.
C) Raza eats only at that restaurant on Fridays.
D) Raza eats at that restaurant only on Fridays.

options.A: Raza only eats at that restaurant on Fridays.
options.B: Only Raza eats at that restaurant on Fridays.
options.C: Raza eats only at that restaurant on Fridays.
options.D: Raza eats at that restaurant only on Fridays.

explanation: 'Only' should be placed immediately before the word or phrase it modifies. To restrict the time to Fridays, 'only' must precede 'on Fridays.' Option A restricts the action (eating), B restricts the person (Raza), and C restricts the location (that restaurant).

question:
Choose the sentence with the correctly placed modifier:
A) Covered in mud, the house was entered by the dog.
B) The dog ran into the house covered in mud.
C) Covered in mud, the dog ran into the house.
D) Running into the house, the dog's mud was visible.

options.A: Covered in mud, the house was entered by the dog.
options.B: The dog ran into the house covered in mud.
options.C: Covered in mud, the dog ran into the house.
options.D: Running into the house, the dog's mud was visible.

explanation: In C, the participial phrase 'Covered in mud' is immediately followed by 'the dog,' the noun it logically modifies. In A, the house appears to be covered in mud. In B, 'covered in mud' ambiguously modifies 'house.' Option D creates a different dangling issue.

question:
Which revision best corrects the dangling modifier in the sentence below?
Original: 'To improve your grades, studying must be done every day.'
A) To improve your grades, studying must be done every day.
B) Studying every day, your grades will improve.
C) To improve your grades, you must study every day.
D) Your grades, studying every day, will improve.

options.A: To improve your grades, studying must be done every day.
options.B: Studying every day, your grades will improve.
options.C: To improve your grades, you must study every day.
options.D: Your grades, studying every day, will improve.

explanation: The infinitive phrase 'To improve your grades' must be followed by the agent who will do the improving — a person, not an abstract noun like 'studying.' Only C makes 'you' the subject who must act.

question:
Which revision best corrects the dangling modifier in the sentence below?
Original: 'Having finished the report, the printer was immediately used by Khalid.'
A) Having finished the report, the printer was immediately used by Khalid.
B) Khalid, having finished the report, used the printer immediately.
C) The printer was used immediately by Khalid, having finished the report.
D) Khalid used the printer, having finished the report immediately.

options.A: Having finished the report, the printer was immediately used by Khalid.
options.B: Khalid, having finished the report, used the printer immediately.
options.C: The printer was used immediately by Khalid, having finished the report.
options.D: Khalid used the printer, having finished the report immediately.

explanation: The phrase 'Having finished the report' must logically refer to the person who finished the report — Khalid. Only B places Khalid as the subject immediately after the participial phrase, correctly attaching the modifier.

question:
What is the grammatical problem in the sentence below?
'Students who practice grammar often make fewer mistakes.'
A) 'often' is an incorrect adverb in this context.
B) The sentence contains a squinting modifier — 'often' could modify either 'practice' or 'make fewer mistakes.'
C) 'fewer' should be 'less' because mistakes are countable.
D) There is no grammatical problem; the sentence is correct.

options.A: 'often' is an incorrect adverb in this context.
options.B: The sentence contains a squinting modifier — 'often' could modify either 'practice' or 'make fewer mistakes.'
options.C: 'fewer' should be 'less' because mistakes are countable.
options.D: There is no grammatical problem; the sentence is correct.

explanation: A squinting modifier is placed so it could plausibly modify either the word before it or the word after it. 'Often' here could mean students often practice grammar OR that students make fewer mistakes often. The sentence should be rewritten to clarify: 'Students who often practice grammar make fewer mistakes.'

question:
Which sentence conveys the meaning that every single student in the class came close to failing — but did not actually fail?
A) Almost the entire class failed the exam.
B) The entire class almost failed the exam.
C) The class, almost, entirely failed the exam.
D) The almost entire class failed the exam.

options.A: Almost the entire class failed the exam.
options.B: The entire class almost failed the exam.
options.C: The class, almost, entirely failed the exam.
options.D: The almost entire class failed the exam.

explanation: In B, 'almost' modifies 'failed,' meaning the entire class came very close to failing but did not. In A, 'almost the entire class' means most (but not all) students actually failed. The placement of 'almost' fundamentally changes the meaning.

question:
Which revision best corrects the dangling modifier in the sentence below?
Original: 'Exhausted after the marathon, the medal was awarded to Farhan by the committee.'
A) The medal was awarded to Farhan, exhausted after the marathon, by the committee.
B) Exhausted after the marathon, Farhan was awarded a medal by the committee.
C) After the marathon, exhausted, the medal was awarded to Farhan.
D) Farhan, the medal was awarded to him, exhausted after the marathon.

options.A: The medal was awarded to Farhan, exhausted after the marathon, by the committee.
options.B: Exhausted after the marathon, Farhan was awarded a medal by the committee.
options.C: After the marathon, exhausted, the medal was awarded to Farhan.
options.D: Farhan, the medal was awarded to him, exhausted after the marathon.

explanation: The participial phrase 'Exhausted after the marathon' logically describes Farhan, not the medal or the committee. B places Farhan immediately after the modifier, correctly attaching it to the person it describes.

question:
Identify the problem in the sentence below and select the best correction:
'The professor explained the theory to the students using complicated diagrams.'
A) No problem — the sentence is grammatically correct as written.
B) 'using complicated diagrams' is a misplaced modifier implying the students used diagrams; correct version: 'Using complicated diagrams, the professor explained the theory to the students.'
C) 'to the students' should be removed as redundant.
D) 'complicated' is imprecise; replace it with 'complex,' but no structural change is needed.

options.A: No problem — the sentence is grammatically correct as written.
options.B: 'using complicated diagrams' is a misplaced modifier implying the students used diagrams; correct version: 'Using complicated diagrams, the professor explained the theory to the students.'
options.C: 'to the students' should be removed as redundant.
options.D: 'complicated' is imprecise; replace it with 'complex,' but no structural change is needed.

explanation: In the original sentence, 'using complicated diagrams' follows 'students,' creating the implication that the students used the diagrams. Moving the participial phrase to the beginning of the sentence correctly attaches it to 'the professor,' who is the one using the diagrams.

question:
Which revision most effectively corrects the dangling modifier in the sentence below?
Original: 'While driving to work, the accident occurred at the intersection.'
A) While driving to work, I witnessed the accident at the intersection.
B) Driving to work while, the accident occurred at the intersection.
C) The accident, while I was driving to work, occurred at the intersection.
D) At the intersection, driving to work, the accident occurred.

options.A: While driving to work, I witnessed the accident at the intersection.
options.B: Driving to work while, the accident occurred at the intersection.
options.C: The accident, while I was driving to work, occurred at the intersection.
options.D: At the intersection, driving to work, the accident occurred.

explanation: The original sentence implies that the accident was driving to work. A correctly restructures the sentence so that 'I' — the implied driver — becomes the subject immediately following the modifier. C, while grammatically functional, uses a full subordinate clause rather than fixing the participial phrase, and is more awkward.

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'Neither the manager nor the employees was present at the meeting.'
A) Neither the manager nor the employees was present at the meeting.
B) Neither the manager nor the employees were present at the meeting.
C) Neither the manager nor the employees is present at the meeting.
D) Neither the manager nor the employees has been present at the meeting.

options.A: Neither the manager nor the employees was present at the meeting.
options.B: Neither the manager nor the employees were present at the meeting.
options.C: Neither the manager nor the employees is present at the meeting.
options.D: Neither the manager nor the employees has been present at the meeting.

explanation: With 'neither...nor,' the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. The closer subject is 'employees,' which is plural, so the verb must be plural: 'were.' The original uses the singular 'was,' which is incorrect.

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'She don't know the answer to the question.'
A) She don't know the answer to the question.
B) She doesn't knows the answer to the question.
C) She doesn't know the answer to the question.
D) She do not knows the answer to the question.

options.A: She don't know the answer to the question.
options.B: She doesn't knows the answer to the question.
options.C: She doesn't know the answer to the question.
options.D: She do not knows the answer to the question.

explanation: The third-person singular subject 'She' requires the auxiliary 'does not' (contracted as 'doesn't'). The base form of the main verb ('know') follows the auxiliary. 'Don't' is only correct with I/you/we/they.

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'Between you and I, the project is significantly behind schedule.'
A) Between you and I, the project is significantly behind schedule.
B) Between I and you, the project is significantly behind schedule.
C) Between you and me, the project is significantly behind schedule.
D) Among you and me, the project is significantly behind schedule.

options.A: Between you and I, the project is significantly behind schedule.
options.B: Between I and you, the project is significantly behind schedule.
options.C: Between you and me, the project is significantly behind schedule.
options.D: Among you and me, the project is significantly behind schedule.

explanation: Prepositions (such as 'between') require the objective case for pronouns. Therefore, 'me' is correct, not 'I.' Option D is wrong because 'among' is used for three or more; 'between' is correct for two parties.

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'She works more harder than anyone else in the office.'
A) She works more harder than anyone else in the office.
B) She works most harder than anyone else in the office.
C) She works harder than anyone else in the office.
D) She works more hard than anyone else in the office.

options.A: She works more harder than anyone else in the office.
options.B: She works most harder than anyone else in the office.
options.C: She works harder than anyone else in the office.
options.D: She works more hard than anyone else in the office.

explanation: 'More harder' is a double comparative, which is non-standard English. One-syllable adjectives and adverbs form comparatives with the suffix '-er' ('harder'), not with 'more.' The correct form is simply 'harder.'

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'He is one of those students who always completes their homework on time.'
A) He is one of those students who always completes their homework on time.
B) He is one of those students who always complete their homework on time.
C) He is one of those students who is always completing their homework on time.
D) He is one of those students whose always completing their homework on time.

options.A: He is one of those students who always completes their homework on time.
options.B: He is one of those students who always complete their homework on time.
options.C: He is one of those students who is always completing their homework on time.
options.D: He is one of those students whose always completing their homework on time.

explanation: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'students' (plural), not to 'one' (singular). Therefore, the verb must be plural: 'complete,' not 'completes.' The full antecedent of 'who' is 'those students,' which governs the verb agreement.

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'The reason for the delay is because the supplier failed to deliver on time.'
A) The reason for the delay is because the supplier failed to deliver on time.
B) The reason for the delay is that the supplier failed to deliver on time.
C) The delay's reason is because the supplier's failure was to deliver on time.
D) The reason is because of the delay caused by the supplier's failure.

options.A: The reason for the delay is because the supplier failed to deliver on time.
options.B: The reason for the delay is that the supplier failed to deliver on time.
options.C: The delay's reason is because the supplier's failure was to deliver on time.
options.D: The reason is because of the delay caused by the supplier's failure.

explanation: 'The reason is because' is redundant because 'because' introduces a causal clause which restates 'reason.' The standard construction is 'The reason is that,' which introduces a noun clause identifying the reason without repeating the idea of cause.

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'The data clearly show that carbon levels has risen dramatically in recent decades.'
A) The data clearly show that carbon levels has risen dramatically in recent decades.
B) The data clearly shows that carbon levels have risen dramatically in recent decades.
C) The data clearly show that carbon levels have risen dramatically in recent decades.
D) The datas clearly show that carbon levels have risen dramatically in recent decades.

options.A: The data clearly show that carbon levels has risen dramatically in recent decades.
options.B: The data clearly shows that carbon levels have risen dramatically in recent decades.
options.C: The data clearly show that carbon levels have risen dramatically in recent decades.
options.D: The datas clearly show that carbon levels have risen dramatically in recent decades.

explanation: 'Data' is the plural form of 'datum' and takes a plural verb: 'show,' not 'shows.' 'Carbon levels' is also plural and takes 'have risen.' Option D introduces a non-existent word ('datas'). C corrects both agreement errors in the original.

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'The committee is comprised of twelve members from various departments.'
A) The committee is comprised of twelve members from various departments.
B) The committee comprises of twelve members from various departments.
C) The committee is composed of twelve members from various departments.
D) The committee is composing twelve members from various departments.

options.A: The committee is comprised of twelve members from various departments.
options.B: The committee comprises of twelve members from various departments.
options.C: The committee is composed of twelve members from various departments.
options.D: The committee is composing twelve members from various departments.

explanation: 'Comprise' means 'to consist of'; the whole comprises the parts. 'Is comprised of' is widely considered incorrect because it reverses the relationship. The correct constructions are 'The committee comprises twelve members' or 'The committee is composed of twelve members.' C is the correctly worded passive alternative.

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'Irregardless of the outcome, the committee decided to proceed with the original plan.'
A) Irregardless of the outcome, the committee decided to proceed with the original plan.
B) Disregardless of the outcome, the committee decided to proceed with the original plan.
C) Regardless of the outcome, the committee decided to proceed with the original plan.
D) Irregardless of the outcome, the committee will decide to proceed with the original plan.

options.A: Irregardless of the outcome, the committee decided to proceed with the original plan.
options.B: Disregardless of the outcome, the committee decided to proceed with the original plan.
options.C: Regardless of the outcome, the committee decided to proceed with the original plan.
options.D: Irregardless of the outcome, the committee will decide to proceed with the original plan.

explanation: 'Irregardless' is a non-standard word formed by incorrectly combining 'irrespective' and 'regardless.' The negative prefix 'ir-' and the negative suffix '-less' cancel each other out, making the word illogical. The standard word is 'regardless.'

question:
Choose the option that corrects the grammatical error in the sentence below:
Original: 'The number of applicants who have submitted incomplete forms are surprisingly high.'
A) The number of applicants who have submitted incomplete forms are surprisingly high.
B) The number of applicants who have submitted incomplete forms is surprisingly high.
C) The number of applicants having submitted incomplete forms are surprisingly high.
D) A number of applicants who submitted incomplete forms is surprisingly high.

options.A: The number of applicants who have submitted incomplete forms are surprisingly high.
options.B: The number of applicants who have submitted incomplete forms is surprisingly high.
options.C: The number of applicants having submitted incomplete forms are surprisingly high.
options.D: A number of applicants who submitted incomplete forms is surprisingly high.

explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb ('is'), because the subject of the main clause is 'number,' not 'applicants.' By contrast, 'a number of' takes a plural verb. The relative clause 'who have submitted' correctly uses a plural verb agreeing with 'applicants,' its own antecedent.

question:
Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence:
'A number of students _____ absent from class today.'
A) is
B) are
C) was
D) has been

options.A: is
options.B: are
options.C: was
options.D: has been

explanation: The expression 'a number of' functions as a quantifier meaning 'several' or 'many' and takes a plural verb. This contrasts with 'the number of,' which takes a singular verb because the head noun is 'number.' Here, 'are' is the correct plural verb.

question:
Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence:
'The professor, along with her two research assistants, _____ presenting findings at the international conference.'
A) are
B) were
C) is
D) have been

options.A: are
options.B: were
options.C: is
options.D: have been

explanation: The true subject is 'professor,' which is singular. The phrase 'along with her two research assistants' is a parenthetical addition — it does not change the number of the subject. Parenthetical phrases introduced by 'along with,' 'as well as,' or 'in addition to' do not make a singular subject plural.

question:
Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence:
'Either the director or the lead producers _____ responsible for approving the final cut of the film.'
A) is
B) are
C) was
D) has been

options.A: is
options.B: are
options.C: was
options.D: has been

explanation: With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor' constructions, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it (the principle of proximity). The closer subject is 'lead producers,' which is plural; therefore the correct verb is 'are.'

question:
Choose the sentence that correctly uses parallel structure:
A) She enjoys hiking, to swim, and reading novels.
B) She enjoys hiking, swimming, and to read novels.
C) She enjoys hiking, swimming, and reading novels.
D) She enjoys to hike, swimming, and reading novels.

options.A: She enjoys hiking, to swim, and reading novels.
options.B: She enjoys hiking, swimming, and to read novels.
options.C: She enjoys hiking, swimming, and reading novels.
options.D: She enjoys to hike, swimming, and reading novels.

explanation: Parallel structure requires that all items in a series use the same grammatical form. In C, all three items are gerunds (hiking, swimming, reading), creating a grammatically parallel list. All other options mix gerunds and infinitives.

question:
Choose the sentence that best corrects the parallelism error:
Original: 'The new policy requires employees to submit reports weekly, attend monthly training sessions, and their performance will be evaluated quarterly.'
A) The new policy requires employees to submit reports weekly, attend monthly training sessions, and their performance will be evaluated quarterly.
B) The new policy requires employees to submit reports weekly, to attend monthly training sessions, and for performance evaluation to happen quarterly.
C) The new policy requires employees to submit reports weekly, attend monthly training sessions, and have their performance evaluated quarterly.
D) The new policy requires employees submitting reports weekly, attending training sessions monthly, and evaluating their performance quarterly.

options.A: The new policy requires employees to submit reports weekly, attend monthly training sessions, and their performance will be evaluated quarterly.
options.B: The new policy requires employees to submit reports weekly, to attend monthly training sessions, and for performance evaluation to happen quarterly.
options.C: The new policy requires employees to submit reports weekly, attend monthly training sessions, and have their performance evaluated quarterly.
options.D: The new policy requires employees submitting reports weekly, attending training sessions monthly, and evaluating their performance quarterly.

explanation: C creates a parallel series of bare infinitives following 'requires employees to': submit... attend... have [their performance evaluated]. The third element in A shifts to an independent clause, breaking the parallel structure. B uses inconsistent forms. D changes the meaning by making employees the ones evaluating.

question:
Choose the sentence that uses correlative conjunctions with correct parallel structure:
A) Not only did she excel in academics, but also in sports she was remarkable.
B) Not only was she excelling in academics, but also sports were her strength.
C) She excelled not only in academics but also in sports.
D) Not only she excelled in academics but also sports.

options.A: Not only did she excel in academics, but also in sports she was remarkable.
options.B: Not only was she excelling in academics, but also sports were her strength.
options.C: She excelled not only in academics but also in sports.
options.D: Not only she excelled in academics but also sports.

explanation: Correlative conjunctions ('not only...but also') require the same grammatical structure after each conjunction. In C, both elements are prepositional phrases: 'in academics' and 'in sports,' creating perfect parallel structure. A and B have mismatched structures after the conjunctions.

question:
Choose the sentence that best corrects the parallelism error:
Original: 'The audit report criticized the firm for failing to disclose financial risks, not maintaining proper records, and the oversight of regulatory compliance was found to be inadequate.'
A) The audit report criticized the firm for failing to disclose financial risks, not maintaining proper records, and the oversight of regulatory compliance was found to be inadequate.
B) The audit report criticized the firm for failing to disclose financial risks, not maintaining proper records, and inadequately overseeing regulatory compliance.
C) The audit report criticized the firm for its failure in disclosing financial risks, maintaining records improperly, and oversight of regulatory compliance being inadequate.
D) The audit report criticized the firm for financial risk non-disclosure, improper record maintenance, and inadequacy in regulatory compliance oversight.

options.A: The audit report criticized the firm for failing to disclose financial risks, not maintaining proper records, and the oversight of regulatory compliance was found to be inadequate.
options.B: The audit report criticized the firm for failing to disclose financial risks, not maintaining proper records, and inadequately overseeing regulatory compliance.
options.C: The audit report criticized the firm for its failure in disclosing financial risks, maintaining records improperly, and oversight of regulatory compliance being inadequate.
options.D: The audit report criticized the firm for financial risk non-disclosure, improper record maintenance, and inadequacy in regulatory compliance oversight.

explanation: B creates a parallel series of three gerund phrases following 'for': 'failing to disclose...,' 'not maintaining...,' and 'inadequately overseeing...' The original (A) breaks the pattern with an independent clause. C mixes gerunds with a nominalized phrase. D uses nouns, which is structurally parallel but changes the register awkwardly.

question:
Choose the sentence with consistent verb tense:
A) She walked into the room and greets everyone with a warm smile.
B) She walks into the room and greeted everyone with a warm smile.
C) She walked into the room and greeted everyone with a warm smile.
D) She had walked into the room and greets everyone with a warm smile.

options.A: She walked into the room and greets everyone with a warm smile.
options.B: She walks into the room and greeted everyone with a warm smile.
options.C: She walked into the room and greeted everyone with a warm smile.
options.D: She had walked into the room and greets everyone with a warm smile.

explanation: Both verbs describe actions in the same narrative sequence, so they must be in the same tense. C correctly uses past tense throughout: 'walked' and 'greeted.' All other options mix past and present tenses, creating inconsistency.

question:
Which statement is correct about the following sentence?
'By the time the investigators arrived, the suspect had already destroyed all the evidence.'
A) The sentence is incorrect; it should use 'already destroyed' without 'had' since 'arrived' is past tense.
B) The sentence is incorrect; 'had destroyed' should be 'has destroyed' to match the perfect aspect.
C) The sentence is grammatically correct; past perfect 'had destroyed' correctly indicates the earlier of two past events.
D) The sentence is incorrect; 'had already destroyed' is redundant — 'already' and past perfect cannot be used together.

options.A: The sentence is incorrect; it should use 'already destroyed' without 'had' since 'arrived' is past tense.
options.B: The sentence is incorrect; 'had destroyed' should be 'has destroyed' to match the perfect aspect.
options.C: The sentence is grammatically correct; past perfect 'had destroyed' correctly indicates the earlier of two past events.
options.D: The sentence is incorrect; 'had already destroyed' is redundant — 'already' and past perfect cannot be used together.

explanation: The past perfect ('had destroyed') is used to express an action completed before another past action ('arrived'). This is its standard use. 'Already' emphasizes the completion and is perfectly compatible with the past perfect. The sentence is grammatically correct.

question:
Choose the sentence that uses the correct tense in the conditional clause:
A) If she studies hard, she would pass the entrance examination.
B) If she studied hard, she will pass the entrance examination.
C) If she studies hard, she will pass the entrance examination.
D) If she would study hard, she will pass the entrance examination.

options.A: If she studies hard, she would pass the entrance examination.
options.B: If she studied hard, she will pass the entrance examination.
options.C: If she studies hard, she will pass the entrance examination.
options.D: If she would study hard, she will pass the entrance examination.

explanation: For real/open conditionals (first conditional), the pattern is: 'If + present simple, ... will + base verb.' This expresses a genuine possibility. C follows this pattern correctly. A mixes present with 'would' (second conditional pattern). B mixes past with 'will.' D incorrectly uses 'would' in the if-clause.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question.

Passage: 'The Amazon rainforest, often called the lungs of the Earth, produces approximately twenty percent of the world's oxygen through photosynthesis. Home to more than three million species of plants and animals, it is the most biodiverse region on the planet. However, deforestation driven by agricultural expansion and logging has destroyed nearly seventeen percent of the forest over the last fifty years. Scientists warn that if deforestation continues at its current rate, the ecosystem could reach a tipping point within decades, transforming large sections of the rainforest into dry savanna.'

According to the passage, what percentage of the world's oxygen does the Amazon rainforest produce?
A) Ten percent
B) Seventeen percent
C) Twenty percent
D) Fifty percent

options.A: Ten percent
options.B: Seventeen percent
options.C: Twenty percent
options.D: Fifty percent

explanation: The passage explicitly states that the Amazon rainforest 'produces approximately twenty percent of the world's oxygen through photosynthesis.' Seventeen percent refers to the portion of the forest already destroyed by deforestation.

question:
Refer to the passage from question d03_v_031 (Amazon rainforest passage).

What does the author most likely mean by the phrase 'tipping point' as used in the passage?
A) A point at which the rainforest suddenly gains additional biodiversity.
B) A critical threshold beyond which environmental damage becomes self-sustaining and potentially irreversible.
C) The moment scientists decided to begin studying deforestation.
D) A political turning point at which governments agree to stop logging.

options.A: A point at which the rainforest suddenly gains additional biodiversity.
options.B: A critical threshold beyond which environmental damage becomes self-sustaining and potentially irreversible.
options.C: The moment scientists decided to begin studying deforestation.
options.D: A political turning point at which governments agree to stop logging.

explanation: In context, 'tipping point' refers to a threshold beyond which the system shifts dramatically — the rainforest transforming into dry savanna. This implies the damage would be self-perpetuating and difficult to reverse. The word is used in its technical/scientific sense to describe a non-linear ecological transition.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question.

Passage: 'Urban heat islands form when cities replace natural land cover with dense concentrations of pavement, buildings, and other surfaces that absorb and retain heat. Temperatures in urban areas can be up to five degrees Celsius higher than in surrounding rural areas. This temperature differential increases energy consumption, elevates air pollution levels, and adversely affects public health. Green roofs, urban forests, and reflective pavements have been proposed as cost-effective mitigation strategies, though their large-scale implementation remains a logistical challenge for many municipalities.'

Which of the following best describes the author's tone in this passage?
A) Alarmist and emotionally charged
B) Dismissive of urban environmental concerns
C) Objective and informative
D) Enthusiastically optimistic about urban planning solutions

options.A: Alarmist and emotionally charged
options.B: Dismissive of urban environmental concerns
options.C: Objective and informative
options.D: Enthusiastically optimistic about urban planning solutions

explanation: The author presents factual information about urban heat islands — their causes, effects, and proposed solutions — without emotional language or personal bias. The acknowledgment that implementation 'remains a logistical challenge' shows balance rather than enthusiasm or alarm. The tone is consistently neutral and informative.

question:
Refer to the passage from question d03_v_033 (urban heat islands passage).

In the final sentence of the passage, the word 'mitigation' most nearly means:
A) The complete elimination of a problem
B) The worsening or intensification of a problem
C) The reduction or lessening of the severity of a problem
D) The documentation and recording of a problem for future study

options.A: The complete elimination of a problem
options.B: The worsening or intensification of a problem
options.C: The reduction or lessening of the severity of a problem
options.D: The documentation and recording of a problem for future study

explanation: 'Mitigation' means to make something less severe, serious, or painful. In the passage, the strategies (green roofs, urban forests, reflective pavements) are proposed to reduce — not eliminate — the heat island effect. This aligns with the precise meaning of mitigation as partial relief rather than complete solution.

question:

B) Indifferent

options.B: Indifferent
options.C: Kind-hearted
options.D: Aggressive

question:

options.B: Garrulous
options.C: Reticent
options.D: Laconic

question:

options.B: Momentary
options.C: Transient
options.D: Enduring

question:

options.B: Pessimistic

'Optimistic' is its closest synonym. 'Melancholic' and 'pessimistic' are antonyms; 'indolent' means lazy.

question:

question:

question:

question:

The word 'equivocal' most nearly means:

question:

question:

B) Confusion
C) Memory
D) Persuasion

options.B: Confusion
options.C: Memory
options.D: Persuasion

explanation: The relationship is: verb means 'to destroy or diminish' its paired noun. 'Enervate' means to drain one of vitality; 'obfuscate' means to obscure or destroy clarity. Just as enervating something removes its vitality, obfuscating something removes its clarity. The answer is the thing that obfuscation takes away.

question:
Read the argument and answer the question.

Argument: 'Schools should ban smartphones because research shows that students who use smartphones during class perform worse academically than students who do not use them.'

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens this argument?
A) Smartphones can be effectively used as educational tools in some classroom activities.
B) Students who already perform poorly academically are significantly more likely to use smartphones during class out of disengagement.
C) Many schools already have partial smartphone restriction policies in place.
D) Educational apps available on smartphones are sometimes less expensive than traditional textbooks.

options.A: Smartphones can be effectively used as educational tools in some classroom activities.
options.B: Students who already perform poorly academically are significantly more likely to use smartphones during class out of disengagement.
options.C: Many schools already have partial smartphone restriction policies in place.
options.D: Educational apps available on smartphones are sometimes less expensive than traditional textbooks.

explanation: The argument assumes that smartphone use causes poor performance. Option B introduces reverse causation: poor academic performance causes students to disengage and use smartphones, not the reverse. This fundamentally undermines the causal claim in the argument. A and D suggest positive uses for phones but do not challenge the causal logic. C is irrelevant to the causal claim.

question:
Read the argument and identify the hidden assumption.

Argument: 'Crime rates in Metropolis fell by thirty percent in the year after the new community policing strategy was implemented. Therefore, the new policing strategy caused the reduction in crime.'

The argument above relies on which of the following assumptions?
A) The city council that approved the strategy is knowledgeable about criminology.
B) No other factors — such as economic improvement or demographic changes — contributed to the reduction in crime rates.
C) A thirty-percent reduction in crime is a statistically meaningful and significant figure.
D) The community policing strategy was implemented uniformly across all districts of Metropolis.

options.A: The city council that approved the strategy is knowledgeable about criminology.
options.B: No other factors — such as economic improvement or demographic changes — contributed to the reduction in crime rates.
options.C: A thirty-percent reduction in crime is a statistically meaningful and significant figure.
options.D: The community policing strategy was implemented uniformly across all districts of Metropolis.

explanation: The argument commits the post hoc fallacy — assuming that because B followed A, A caused B. For this causal conclusion to hold, the argument must assume that no confounding variables (economic shifts, seasonal trends, demographic changes) explain the drop. B identifies this hidden assumption. Without it, the argument from mere correlation to causation collapses.
